<reason>A narrowly won a high-quality exchange. B's two live routes — unworkable enforcement (ministerial-exception deference, entanglement) and redundancy ("safe where redundant, unpoliced where dangerous") — were genuinely damaging and A only partially answered the entanglement version. But A controlled the two most decisive clashes: A's dilemma question on children forced B into a "uniforms yes, religious norms no" position, and A's closing rejoinder that children cannot consent to anything (boarding school, piano, vegetarianism) and that parents mediate choice everywhere went unanswered, exposing B's consent standard as selectively anti-religious. A also defused B's hard-case examples early by showing they fall outside the motion's own conditions, and the "we litigate hard lines like undue hardship" analogy plus "fix review, don't abolish the right" gave a coherent answer to the enforcement worry. B's redundancy reframe arrived late and never fully absorbed A's opening anti-ban scenario. A's Rebuttal 2 was clipped, an execution cost, but its A1/A2 answers were substantively responsive. Net: A made the debate easier to decide on the motion as written.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>The children-consent exchange: A's pressure question pinned B into conceding uniforms but rejecting religious norms, and A's closing — that parental choice mediates every childhood decision and dress is not a unique exception — decisively undercut B's consent-based objection, which B never rebutted.</best_rebuttal>
